title: Memes for 2030

sourceEvidence.locator: Naming a future already under pressure
sourceEvidence.excerpt: The book is written for readers who want to attach their names to consequential ideas rather than merely occupy attention. Its theory of fame is demanding: durable recognition comes when a person supplies language that strangers need in order to understand their own circumstances. Ideas become powerful when dispersed private discomfort gains a public sentence, when existing institutions no longer make an experience intelligible and when a compact proposition gives repeaters both an explanation and a role. Cultural timing matters as much as abstract correctness.

sourceEvidence.locator: Naming a future already under pressure
sourceEvidence.excerpt: A successful meme, in this usage, is not simply a viral joke or marketing slogan. It compresses a real moral pressure into language simple enough to travel without becoming intellectually empty. It must feel surprising and already obvious, invite debate beyond the moment of repetition and point toward a form of life. The ten proposals are therefore open prototypes rather than deterministic forecasts. Their value depends on truth, transmissibility, institutional adoption and the quality of conduct they make imaginable—not raw visibility alone.

sourceEvidence.locator: Human agency and a verifiable world
sourceEvidence.excerpt: “Humanity Is Not a Bug” answers automation without demanding technological retreat. As machines outperform people across more tasks, human presence may become a protected mark of dignity in consequential decisions, education, medicine, hospitality, law and art. The point is not that humans are always more accurate. It is that responsibility, improvisation, empathy and the right to contest a decision can matter independently of optimized performance. An advanced society may distinguish carefully between work machines should relieve and places where people must remain answerable.

sourceEvidence.locator: Human agency and a verifiable world
sourceEvidence.excerpt: “Reality Is the New Luxury” responds to synthetic media and effortless fabrication. Scarcity shifts from content toward provenance: confidence that an event occurred, a voice belongs to someone, an object has a history and a promise is owned by an accountable person. Reality need not mean untouched by technology. It means anchored in traceable consequences and open to verification. The phrase becomes politically significant when authentication, chain of custody and trustworthy institutions are made emotionally meaningful rather than reduced to technical badges available only to experts.

hook: Someone gives a familiar frustration a name, and suddenly strangers can act together.
readerPromise: See how language can connect private discomfort with responsible collective action.
protectedRevelations: Detailed adoption strategies, comparisons, final impact judgments.
visualPlan: A phrase people needed: A neighbor recognizes the worker’s neglected repair and pauses beside the same bridge. Reveal the book beside this ordinary encounter, naming the collection of ten ideas.
The work behind the words: Follow the same repaired joint as both people look at the work it needed. Let the repairer tighten one joint while the neighbor acknowledges the effort.
Permission to disappear: A reader puts a phone down beside a bench without an alarm or celebration. Hold the reader’s choice as a shared practice becomes possible in the background.
Ideas with a public life: An artist and neighbor consider an unfinished public mark on a wall. End with the brush still in hand, leaving the shared idea unfinished.

visualActionChanges.direction: Open on the bridge and unrecognized maintenance worker; let recognition arrive with the public phrase.
Keep one repair action on the joint and spanner, removing later repetitive gestures.
Let the phone become quiet beside the reader; hold the bench scene for the freedom to be unavailable.
Use the shared wall and two people as the invitation to carry an idea into public life.
